summary: Describes two ways to route voice messages using a telephone number. The complete service uses the VPIM directory to look up an email address and confirm it belongs to the intended recipient. A simpler fallback, described as send-and-pray, uses only ENUM and ordinary DNS mail routing to deliver messages.

plainLanguage.summary: This document explains how to route a voice message when you know only a telephone number. It describes two ways. The careful way checks a directory for the right email address. The simple way builds an address from a fixed rule and leaves the rest to the recipient's mail system.

questions: route voice messages by telephone number
what is send and pray voice messaging
how does enum route voice messages
subtitle: Two ways to reach a voice mailbox when all you know is a telephone number.

tldr.problem: Voice messages are addressed by telephone number, but Internet mail needs an email address, so a sender needs a way to turn a number into a mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: The complete service uses ENUM to find the VPIM directory and LDAP to fetch the confirmed email address; the basic send-and-pray service uses NAPTR rewrite rules to build an address and ordinary MX routing to deliver it.
tldr.outcome: The complete service confirms that the address is valid and belongs to the intended recipient, while the basic service offers no such guarantee. RFC 6118 later updated this document.

today: RFC 4238 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 6118.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 4238 profiles two mechanisms for routing messages that are addressed by a telephone number. The most complete service uses the ENUM address resolution service to determine the VPIM directory, then uses LDAP to retrieve the VPIM-specific email address that will be used for routing. The more basic send-and-pray service uses only ENUM and MX records to route the message to the recipient's domain, leaving the intelligence to route it further inside that domain to the domain's own message routing system.

The basic mechanism may be used even when a VPIM directory service is available. It is useful when LDAP queries are not available, such as with disconnected mobile terminals or because of firewall or information security policies. The design aims to avoid any content processing to determine the nature of the message and its internal destination. At a minimum, it should be possible to establish a simple mail forwarding rule that sends all inbound VPIM messages to a designated system, while routing FAX, SMS, or other telephone-addressed messages to other, potentially different, systems.

The mechanisms are meant to be extensible to all store-and-forward, telephone-number addressed messaging services. A timing goal also applies: the VPIM directory discovery and VPIM directory query steps should occur within the timing constraints for user interfaces in PSTN networks, where the constraint can be a two-second response 95% of the time.
sections.plainLanguage: The document sets out two ways to route a voice message from a phone number. The careful way looks up an email address in a directory. The simple way builds an address by rule and lets the recipient's mail system sort it out. Both must be fast: the RFC sets a goal of a two-second answer 95% of the time.

sections.title: The Complete Service
sections.content:
For the complete VPIM message routing service, the sending client SHOULD query the VPIM directory for the VPIM-specific email address. The client SHOULD use the ENUM service to retrieve the identity of the VPIM directory to query, and then query that server for the email address and any additional attributes desired.

The service is registered as E2U+VPIM:LDAP, with URI type LDAP:, type VPIM, subtype LDAP and intended usage COMMON. Because the address comes from a directory, this service both finds the mailbox and confirms that the address is valid and associated with the intended recipient. The RFC notes that this service will take time to become widely deployed in the near term.
sections.plainLanguage: The complete service makes two lookups before the message is sent. First the sender asks the DNS which directory holds voice messaging details for that number. Then it asks that directory for the email address of the person. Because the address comes from a directory, the sender learns that it is valid and belongs to the intended recipient.

sections.title: VPIM Directory Discovery
sections.content:
The VPIM directory server is found by using the ENUM protocol and querying for the VPIMDIR service associated with the telephone number of the recipient. The DNS query name is created as described by RFC 3761. The telephone number used for the directory location MAY contain additional sub-address information as additional digits.

The answer is one or more NAPTR records holding LDAP URLs. It is recommended that VPIMDIR servers be deployed in a redundant configuration. The NAPTR weight fields provide the ability to give two records indicating the same service and preference a different weight, and the same weight can be specified for random distribution between the two servers.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender looks the number up in the DNS using the ENUM service defined in RFC 3761. The answer is a NAPTR record that names a directory server. A number may carry extra digits for a sub-address. The RFC recommends running more than one directory server and using the NAPTR weight field to decide how requests are shared.

sections.title: The Address Query
sections.content:
Once the VPIM directory is discovered, the client SHOULD issue an LDAP query for vPIMrFC822Mailbox, that is, the address that SHOULD be used as the value for both the RFC 822 To: field and the SMTP RCPT command, as described in RFC 4237.

This lookup is what makes the service complete. The address is not assembled from a rule; the directory states it, so the sender can check that it is valid and that it belongs to the intended recipient. The client may also ask for any additional attributes it wants while it is querying the same server.
sections.plainLanguage: With the directory server known, the sender asks it for the attribute named vPIMrFC822Mailbox. The value is the email address to use, both in the message's To: field and in the SMTP RCPT command.

sections.title: The Basic Send-and-Pray Service
sections.content:
The basic service relies upon NAPTR rewrite rules to mechanically construct a VPIM-specific email address. It is registered as E2U+VPIM:Mailto:, with URI type Mailto:, type VPIM and subtype MAILTO. To facilitate a full range of intradomain routing options, the constructed address indicates that the message is a VPIM message, and that indication SHOULD be in the domain name portion of the address, for ease of processing in the recipient's intradomain mail routing system.

The address is constructed using the address rewrite rules of the NAPTR records associated with the VPIM service. There is no assurance that the constructed address is valid, nor that the constructed address corresponds to the intended recipient. Because no capabilities information is provided about the recipient, messages sent with this mechanism SHOULD be sent using only the media and content types of the VPIM V2 profile, defined in RFC 3801.

The RFC lists three error conditions for the service: the E.164 number is not in the numbering plan, the E.164 number is in the numbering plan but no URLs exist for that number, or the E2U+VPIM:Mailto service is unavailable.
sections.plainLanguage: The basic service skips the directory. It uses a rewrite rule from the DNS to build an email address from the phone number, and the rule marks the address as a voice message. Nothing checks that the address is valid or belongs to the intended person, so the sender should use only the media types of the VPIM V2 profile.

sections.title: Routing Inside the Recipient's Domain
sections.content:
The interdomain routing of a constructed VPIM address is mechanically indistinguishable from existing email routing. No changes to the infrastructure are required: the sending system consults the Domain Name System for an MX record corresponding to the domain name and forwards the message to the indicated system.

Within the recipient's domain, the message may be routed further to the appropriate messaging system. The RFC marks this subject as strictly informational, because intradomain routing is an internal matter for the domain and does not affect the protocol. It is only necessary that the addresses created by the NAPTR rewrite rules have meaning to the domain advertising them. Two general mechanisms are described.

  • Directory-enabled routing: an inbound mail router of the recipient's domain uses the local part of the address to query for an internal mail address. That internal mail address is substituted for the SMTP RCPT address and used to deliver the message to the recipient mailbox. The mailbox does not need any knowledge of the mechanically constructed telephone-number-based address. Example address: +12145551212@sp.net.
  • Service-based mail routing: a mail gateway is provisioned with a simple rule or small set of rules to forward all messages of a given service type to a predefined server, checking for the service name VPIM as a prefix to the constructed domain name. That destination may be a single voice messaging server or a service-specific gateway into a larger telephone number-based voice-messaging network. Example address: +12145551212@VPIM.sp.net.
sections.plainLanguage: Between domains, delivery is ordinary email: the sender looks up the domain's MX record and forwards the message. Inside the recipient's domain, the RFC leaves the choice open. A mail router can look up an internal address in a directory, or a single rule can send every voice message to one server.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
There is little information disclosed to the sender of the message that is not already disclosed using standard email protocols. The ability to use this protocol to probe for valid addresses is identical to the sending of test messages and waiting for a non-delivery notification in return.

Two risks are called out. Unsolicited bulk email: the use of ENUM records to create routable email addresses from telephone numbers provides bulk mailers with the capability to send email to a large set of recipients where only the telephone number is known, or where telephone numbers are guessed. DNS-based attacks: both the complete and the basic service rely upon the DNS to provide the information needed to validate a recipient or send a message, and the message sender is a casual, unauthenticated user of the indicated servers. If the DNS is compromised, an attacker can redirect messages by providing a malicious email address or indicating a rogue directory with malicious LDAP URLs.

Use of the DNS security protocols described in RFC 4033 substantially reduces the risk of a domain being hijacked. If the E.164 zone is secured with DNSSEC, the attack is precluded if the client can trust the key used to sign the zone. DNS security does not protect against the LDAP service being independently compromised; the risk to that service is discussed in RFC 4237.
sections.plainLanguage: Both services depend on the DNS, so a tampered DNS can redirect a message to the wrong address. DNSSEC reduces that risk if the client trusts the signing key, but it does nothing if the directory server itself is compromised. Turning phone numbers into email addresses also gives bulk mailers a new list to target.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: This specification registers the E2U+VPIM and E2U+Voice services according to the specifications and guidelines in RFC 3761 and the definitions in this document. Registering the names means that every implementation of either service uses the same strings.
sections.plainLanguage: The document registers the two service names, E2U+VPIM and E2U+Voice, with IANA under the rules in RFC 3761. Registering them means every implementation uses the same names.
